paper_title: IdeaTaste: Do LLMs Share the Research Taste of Human Researchers?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Research taste, the judgment of what to read, which problems to pursue, and which methods to try, increasingly shapes the work of AI scientists, yet it remains far less understood than their ability to execute research. We introduce IdeaTaste, a benchmark that scores an LLM by how closely the research proposals it writes from a literature snapshot frozen at 2025 match the work the same communities published in 2026. Our experiments span six contemporary language models and four research areas from established to emerging fields, covering more than 90{,}000 proposals in total. LLM agents fall well short of human communities in both the literature they cite and the ideas they state, reaching about 26\% of the human level on citation matching and only 18\% on idea matching. Their populations can cite as diversely as a community and take up its tasks and methods, yet rarely arrive at the concrete approaches and research plans it pursues. Neither richer field context nor larger populations substantially close this gap. In blinded expert review, AI proposals trail the 2026 papers least in presentation and most in expected success, echoing their gap in concrete approaches, and those whose ideas no human paper shares fare worst, suggesting weaker directions rather than overlooked opportunities. These results indicate that the main bottleneck in AI research taste lies less in finding the directions a community works on than in turning them into the concrete approaches it goes on to pursue. We release IdeaTaste as an open, continuously updated leaderboard (https://cxcscmu.github.io/IdeaTaste) that benchmarks contemporary AI proposals against future publication cycles.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: AI scientists can now carry out much of the research process on their own, from generating ideas and grounding them in prior work to running experiments and writing papers (Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026; Baek et al., 2025). Frontier laboratories are deploying them at growing scale (OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2026; Gottweis et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026a), and their work has begun to enter the scientific literature (Tang et al., 2026; Bianchi et al., 2026). Yet executing research well matters only when the research itself is worth doing, and this choice rests on research taste, the judgment of what to read, which problems to pursue, and which methods to try. As AI scientists take on larger role in discovery, their taste increasingly shapes the research that comes next, but it remains far less understood than their ability to execute. Evaluating research taste is challenging because it requires reference for which choices are worth making. Existing work mostly judges one idea at time, through expert ratings (Si et al., 2025; 2026), benchmarks with fixed targets (Guo et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025), or model judges that predict which directions will matter (Tian et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Tong et al., 2026), and such judgments are not yet reliable (Sinhahajari et al., 2026; Ho et al., 2026; Baig et al., 2026). Population-level studies find that generated ideas are highly similar within and across models (Jiang et al., 2025; Wenger & Kenett, 2025; Chen et al., 2026b), but they measure how much population repeats itself rather than whether its choices resemble those of human researchers. What is still missing is direct comparison between the research choices of AI scientists and those of the human community working in the same area.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: AI scientists and research agents. AI scientists are now built to run much of the research loop, from idea to experiment to written paper (Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026), and the space is growing quickly (Luo et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025). Agent Laboratory executes human-provided idea, Co-Scientist refines hypotheses through team of agents (Schmidgall et al., 2025; Gottweis et al., 2026), SciAgents and the Virtual Lab carry multi-agent designs into materials and biomedical problems (Ghafarollahi & Buehler, 2025; Swanson et al., 2025), and CycleResearcher adds automated review (Weng et al., 2025). Evaluation has largely followed one unit, single system, even as agent-written work begins to enter the record from deployments at scale and conference with AI authors and reviewers (Tang et al., 2026; Bianchi et al., 2026; Zhong et al., 2026b). This paper moves up level, to population of LLM agents proposing research from one shared literature. Automated idea generation. Within such systems the proposal comes from an ideation step, where methods turn retrieved prior work into problems, hypotheses, and experiment designs (Baek et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025), and related work forecasts active topics from knowledge graph (Krenn et al., 2023; Gu & Krenn, 2025). Ideation has also been run at population scale, on shared archive or inside simulated research community (Schmidgall & Moor, 2025; Yu et al., 2024), where outputs turn out to be substantially similar within and across models (Jiang et al., 2025; Wenger & Kenett, 2025), with further work relating this to knowledge, group size, and crowding against human output (Deng et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Azad & Baten, 2026), as agent societies outside research also develop shared conventions and collective bias (Park et al., 2023; Ashery et al., 2025) and agent ecosystems concentrate into homogeneous offerings (Ling et al., 2026). Such comparisons are mostly internal to the population. This study measures that similarity in the literature proposal cites and in the idea it states, and pairs each with agreement against human papers. Evaluating research ideas. Evaluation supplies the external reference such comparisons lack. Experts judge one idea at time, though the initial advantage of model ideas narrowed once executed (Si et al., 2025; 2026), while benchmarks score ideas against fixed targets (Guo et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025), often leaving the verdict to model judges (Zheng et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025b), now asked which directions will matter (Tian et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026; Tong et al., 2026). Those verdicts are not yet reliable, as judges disagree with experts on novelty (Sinhahajari et al., 2026), trail them at comparison (Baig et al., 2026), and rate unsound ideas as sound (Ho et al., 2026), while human review is itself inconsistent (Cortes & Lawrence, 2021). Published research offers steadier reference, used to score ideas by future impact (Jiang, 2026), to recover heldout paper (Chen et al., 2026c), and to profile ideas against taxonomy on which model output is narrower (Chen et al., 2026d), though citation lists are an imperfect standard (Sahu et al., 2026). This paper extends that reference from single papers to what research community published after its literature was frozen, comparing that with what population cites and proposes.

sections.title: IDEATASTE
sections.content: IdeaTaste evaluates the research taste of LLM agents by comparing the proposals they write from frozen literature with the papers human community later publishes. Sec. 3.1 builds the literature corpus and the human reference, Sec. 3.2 defines four metrics on what each side cites and proposes, and Sec. 3.3 describes the methods.

3.1 DATA CONSTRUCTION
sections.content: We cover four research areas: machine learning systems and code generation, established fields with large literatures, and world models and automated research, smaller fields that are still emerging. For each area, we split the literature at the end of 2025. Papers published through 2025 form the corpus , which LLM agents search and propose from. Papers published in 2026 form the human reference H, which records what the community actually pursued after this cutoff. The cutoff can be moved forward as new papers appear. Both sets are collected by following citations from 20 to 22 landmark papers hand-picked for each area. The corpus first takes in papers published through 2025 that cite landmark and then adds every paper cited by at least two of these citing papers. This second step brings in shared background that may not use the terminology of the area, such as program synthesis work for code generation. The human reference combines 2026 papers that cite landmark with papers returned by topic search, screens them against written area definition, and removes surveys. It covers January to August 2026, and Table 1 reports the sizes of both sets. Appendix gives the area definitions, the landmarks, further construction details, and coverage audit against authoritative surveys.

sections.title: 3.2 EVALUATION DESIGN
sections.content: Writing research document, whether human paper or an LLM agent proposal, involves two choices, selecting the prior work to build on and formulating an idea in relation to it. LLM agents make these choices using only the frozen corpus , while the human reference records the communitys subsequent choices after the cutoff. We therefore compare with the proposals of population at the two corresponding levels (Uzzi et al., 2013; Foster et al., 2015). The resulting information asymmetry across the cutoff is discussed in Appendix E.4. At the citation level, each document is represented by its citation set C(d), the papers it cites that lie in . At the idea level, it is represented by summary that language model extracts from its abstract under fixed schema of five slots I, namely contribution type, problem, motivation, proposed approach, and research plan, as detailed in Appendix B. At each level, matching measures agreement with the human reference and diversity measures how varied the proposals are, giving citation matching MATCH-CITE, citation diversity DIVERSITY-CITE, idea matching MATCH-IDEA, and idea diversity DIVERSITY-IDEA. All four lie in [0, 1], and higher values mean closer agreement with the human reference or greater variety. Applying them to itself, with each human paper compared only with the other human papers, gives the human level against which populations are read.

sections.title: 3.3 METHODS
sections.content: All four methods share one LLM agent implementation and differ only in what it knows about its area. The LLM agent receives the area definition used to screen the human reference and writes one proposal within fixed step budget, taking one action per step: planning, searching the corpus, pinning retrieved papers, revising the draft, compressing its history into notes, or submitting. It can cite only retrieved papers, so its citations always lie in . The methods vary its profile and actions: FREE only states that the LLM agent is researcher in the area, revealing what it pursues without an explicit prior. TOPIC assigns one research topic and leaves the choice of problem open (Lu et al., 2024), testing how broad direction shapes proposals. Topics are allocated in proportion to corpus frequency, with recent years upweighted. LANDSCAPE assigns no topic but lists the areas most common task tags, method tags, and task method pairs with their shares among 2025 papers, plus an action to retrieve papers by tag or pair. It thus exposes the areas structure and how crowded each direction is, which researchers weigh when choosing between established and new directions (Foster et al., 2015). FRONTIER lets LLM agents see one anothers work (Schmidgall & Moor, 2025). It assigns topics like TOPIC but runs in rounds, freezing each rounds proposals and research traces into snapshot that later rounds query through two extra actions, as researchers read peers work. Peer records are separate from literature retrieval, uncitable, and marked as not scientifically validated. These methods test whether an LLM agents view of its area changes the literature and ideas its population selects. See Appendix for more details.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: LLM agents. We run the four methods of Sec. 3.3 in every area with the six language models in Table 2. Each LLM agent has budget of 20 steps, and each population holds 300 proposals, which FRONTIER writes in two rounds of 150. The six models form two groups by design. Four were released in 2026 and power current AI scientists, so their training data may overlap the human reference, but leaving them out would confine the benchmark to outdated models. The other two were trained before 2026 and cannot have seen any 2026 paper, so their results are free of leakage by construction. Comparing the two groups tests whether possible exposure to the reference helps LLM agents anticipate 2026 research. Appendix gives implementation details. Automatic evaluation. All populations are scored with the metrics of Sec. 3.2, and scoring the 2026 papers against one another gives the human level. The slot-level judge is GPT-5.6 Luna, outside the evaluated model families and validated against human annotators in Appendix B.4. Human evaluation. Beyond whether LLM agents propose what the community pursues, we use human evaluation to examine how good their proposals are, and in particular whether those without human counterpart are weak directions or sound ones the community has not yet taken. Eleven reviewers, all with reviewing experience, assess 192 documents without knowing their source. Table 2 scores every population on the four metrics against the human level, and Table 3 reports how reviewers rate blinded sample of proposals and 2026 papers. Together they yield four findings. LLM agents fall far short of the research taste of human communities. On average, LLM agents reach about 26% of the human level on MATCH-CITE and only 18% on MATCH-IDEA, and no population, under any model or in any area, reaches half of it on either metric. The gap is narrowest in automated research, the newest and smallest area, and widens as the area grows, peaking in machine learning systems and code generation. LLM agents thus track community most closely where it has least to choose from and fall furthest behind where it has most. The gap lies in what LLM agents propose, not in what they read. For five of the six models, matching falls further behind the human level on ideas than on citations, and diversity sharpens this split. Once TOPIC or FRONTIER assigns direction, four of the six models cite up to three times as diversely as the community, yet no population reaches the human level of idea diversity. population can thus read as widely as community and still repeat itself in what it proposes, so drawing on the literature community builds on is not enough to arrive at the ideas it pursues. Knowing more, from training or from context, does not close the gap. Although four of the six models may have seen the 2026 papers in training, the two trained before 2026 match more human ideas, about 26% of the human level against 14% as Appendix E.4 details. Idea matching thus follows neither recency nor capability, as Llama 4 Scout matches the most human ideas yet receives the lowest ratings in Table 3. More context does no better. Across the four methods, matching stays within narrow band while citation diversity varies about threefold, so what an LLM agent is told shapes how widely its population spreads far more than how closely it follows human research. The fullest view helps least, as LANDSCAPE ranks last on MATCH-CITE in 19 of 24 settings, while the direction of TOPIC and the peer proposals of FRONTIER broaden population without bringing it near the human level. The quality gap centers on execution and deepens where proposals miss the human record. In blind review, AI proposals score below the 2026 papers on every quality dimension, by 20 points on expected success but only 4 on presentation, so the gap lies less in how the proposals are written than in whether they would work. Reviewers also flag 86% of them as AI-generated, against 39% of the papers. sections.title: 5 ANALYSIS
sections.content: The main results show that LLM agents fall furthest behind on idea matching. We trace where this gap lies, first across research directions, then within the idea summary and in concrete cases, and finally ask whether larger populations close it. Do LLM agents cover the human research directions? Low idea matching may arise because population never takes up the directions the 2026 papers pursue, or because it takes them up and still arrives at different ideas. To tell these apart, we treat direction as task paired with method, that is, what paper works on and how, and label both sides with the task and method vocabulary that LANDSCAPE draws on. We run this comparison for DeepSeek-V4-Flash in automated research, with each population holding as many proposals as the area has papers so that both sides are compared at equal size. Figure 3 reports the share of human tag mass each population reaches. On each axis alone, the populations given direction come close to the community, and FRONTIER misses only small share of the human task mass and of the method mass. On pairs, every population falls away, and even FRONTIER reaches only about half of the human mass, so LLM agents work on the communitys tasks with its methods but combine the two differently. Neither kind of coverage, however, carries over to ideas. FRONTIER reaches about twice the human pair mass of FREE but matches barely more human ideas in Table 2, where the four methods sit within narrow band.

Where do AI and human research ideas differ? To locate the difference inside an idea, we decompose MATCH-IDEA into the slots of the idea summary. Table 4 reports per-slot matching for Llama 4 Scout and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, one model from each side of the 2026 cutoff. Both populations reach the problems and motivations of human papers many times more often than their approaches and research plans, so LLM agents agree with community on what to study and why far more readily than on how to do it. Part of this ordering is intrinsic, since the 2026 papers also match one another far more often on problems than on approaches, an approach being the more specific of the two. Read against this human level, the decline persists for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, which covers small share of human problems and almost none of their research plans, while Llama 4 Scout stays at roughly third of the human level on every slot. Either way, almost no human approach or research plan finds counterpart among the proposals, and this is where the idea gap lies. What do LLM agents propose instead? Figure 4 pairs each of two human papers with two proposals from one language model that share its problem. In both cases, the proposal that misses the human approach leaves the trained network unchanged and adds machinery around it, whereas the human paper and the matching proposal both modify the network itself. The Case 1 paper fine-tunes the router toward expert reuse, while proposal predicts expert demand and prefetches experts around an unchanged network. The Case 2 paper updates low-rank adapters on frozen network, while proposal keeps the weights fixed and adapts through retrieved transitions. The same problem thus admits very different mechanisms, and shared problem does not imply shared approach. Appendix E.9 provides the source schemas and further examples. Can more LLM agents close the gap? If the gap stemmed mainly from population size, sampling more proposals should close it. We grow the FREE and TOPIC populations of Gemini 3.5 FlashLite and DeepSeek-V4-Flash in every area from 300 proposals to the size of the human reference, 3.8 to 17 times larger, and report matching in Figure 5. Matching grows far more slowly than the population. Every curve rises only gently and levels off as proposals accumulate, staying well below the human level even when population holds as many proposals as the community holds papers.

sections.title: Working in Progress
sections.content: Case 1: fetching uncached MoE experts causes substantial I/O overhead. Human ReMoE (Zhu et al., 2026). Fine-tune the router to favor recently used experts, reducing transfers without adding inference-time computation. AI A: approach differs (Qwen3.8-27B, FRONTIER). Predict expert demand from prompt topics, then prefetch experts and coordinate caching and scheduling without changing the model. AI B: approach matches (Qwen3.8-27B, TOPIC). Train only the router to increase expert reuse over consecutive tokens while preserving language-model performance. Case 2: pretrained world models need to adapt to changing environments while retaining prior capabilities. Human SPREAD (Moon & Kim, 2026). Freeze the pretrained model and update low-rank adapters online, aiming for rapid adaptation without replay. AI A: approach differs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, TOPIC). Keep model weights fixed, store observed transitions, and combine retrieved predictions with the models predictions. AI B: approach matches (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, FREE). Adapt frozen model through low-rank updates and compose adapters for combinations of dynamics changes. Figure 4: Two human papers, each paired with two AI proposals from single language model. Under the stored automatic judgments, all four proposals match their human paper on problem and motivation, and only proposal also matches on proposed approach and research plan. Figure 5: Matching against population size. Rows are Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite and DeepSeek-V4Flash from top to bottom, and columns are the four areas. Color marks the method, TOPIC or FREE, and marker shape the level, circles for MATCH-CITE and squares for MATCH-IDEA. An assigned direction helps somewhat, as TOPIC climbs more steeply on ideas than FREE in most settings, yet both remain far from the human level. The gap is thus not an artifact of population size. Together with the analyses above, this shows that neither reaching more of communitys directions nor writing more proposals brings LLM agents closer to the approaches the community arrives at. Improving research taste therefore means improving how recognized problem becomes concrete approach, not how widely or how much population proposes.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduced IdeaTaste, benchmark that measures the research taste of LLM agents against the research human communities go on to publish. Our results point to consistent picture. LLM agents share much of communitys literature and directions, yet seldom arrive at the concrete approaches it pursues, and the proposals that depart from human research tend to be weaker rather than overlooked. This picture holds across newer models, richer context, and larger populations. The research taste of LLM agents is thus limited less by knowing what to work on than by deciding how to pursue it, which we see as the central challenge for future AI scientists.

sections.title: A DATA CONSTRUCTION DETAILS
sections.content: Each area is represented by two sets of papers: corpus of work published through 2025, which is what LLM agents retrieve from, and human reference of papers from 2026, which is what proposals are measured against. The two are built to different standards. The corpus has to be wide enough that the background 2026 paper builds on lies inside it, and it must carry nothing from 2026. The reference set has to be as complete as we can make it and has to hold research in the area. This appendix describes the area definitions, the sources data come from, data construction details, and the survey reference coverage audit. A.1 RESEARCH AREAS Each area is defined in writing before collection begins, and that definition does not change afterwards. It states what belongs to the area and what does not, and it is what every screening step below applies. The LLM agents receive the same text as the description of their research community, so both sides work under one definition of the area. Table 5 gives the four definitions together with the topic search queries used to collect the reference set. Table 5: Area definitions and topic search queries recorded in each areas frozen configuration. Topic search applies to the reference set only.

sections.title: World models
sections.content: Systems research for efficient training and inference of ML and LLM models: inference serving and scheduling, KV-cache and memory management, distributed training and parallelism, quantization, pruning and distillation for efficiency, speculative decoding, efficiency-motivated attention and architecture changes, ML compilers and kernels, hardware acceleration, and MoE systems. Not in scope: architecture work aimed at task quality, downstream applications that merely use these systems, retrieval-augmented generation, alignment, and generic high-performance computing unrelated to ML. Topic search: the OpenAlex topics Parallel Computing and Optimization Techniques and Stochastic Gradient Optimization Techniques, and title and abstract search for llm serving, inference serving, and distributed training. Research on automatically producing program code from natural-language or other specifications with learned models: code LLMs and pretrained code models, program synthesis, natural language to code including text-to-SQL, code benchmarks and code-specific evaluation, program repair and self-debugging, coding agents and LLM-based software engineering, and code data curation. Not in scope: generic LLM and NLP foundation work such as GPT, LLaMA, RLHF and LoRA, generic agent or reasoning work without code focus, generic machine translation metrics, and papers that merely use code as an application domain without studying generation. Topic search: OpenAlex keywords code-generation and program-synthesis. Learned internal models of an environment that represent its current state and predict future states under actions, used for planning and decision-making, simulation, and data generation. A.5 INTERPRETATION OF RESEARCH TASTE. IdeaTaste uses research taste in descriptive sense. research community faces many plausible problems and methods but chooses to pursue only small subset. We therefore treat papers released after the cutoff as observations of these realized research choices. The human reference captures which prior work researchers build on, which problems they pursue, and which approaches they develop. It does not assume that every published paper is high quality or that publication defines scientific value. Accordingly, MATCH-CITE and MATCH-IDEA measure how closely an LLM agent population anticipates the subsequent choices of the corresponding human community. High matching does not by itself imply higher research quality, and low matching does not by itself imply lower quality. The benchmark measures agreement with realized community choices rather than normative standard of scientific merit. The blinded expert study helps interpret the gap beyond matching alone. non-matching proposal could represent valuable direction that the human community did not pursue. However, non-matching AI proposals are judged less feasible and less likely to succeed than non-matching human papers. This suggests that the observed gap is not explained only by different research preferences. We therefore view IdeaTaste as measuring one operational aspect of research taste: whether LLM agents anticipate the research choices that human community later makes. A.

E.4 LEAKAGE AND BENCHMARK ROBUSTNESS Four of the six models in Table 2 were released in 2026 and may have seen part of the reference, which covers January to August 2026, so they could in principle reproduce 2026 papers from memory rather than through research judgment. This choice is deliberate, since benchmark of research taste should evaluate the models that current AI scientists are built on. We pair these releases with two 2025 models whose training data end before the reference year, which gives setting free of exposure within the same benchmark. Below we describe one design constraint that limits exposure, test whether exposure helps, and check whether the findings differ between the two settings. Retrieval restricted to the corpus. An LLM agent cites only papers it retrieves from the corpus of its area, which ends in 2025, so 2026 paper can never enter its citation set. This constraint does not rule out indirect exposure, since model that has read 2026 paper could still reuse its references or restate its idea. The test below addresses this remaining channel. Models released before and after the reference year. Meta reports an August 2024 pretraining cutoff for Llama 4 Scout, and Anthropic reports that the public internet data of Claude Haiku 4.5 end in February 2025 (Meta AI, 2025b; Anthropic, 2025b). Neither can have seen paper first released in 2026, so the two serve as temporal controls for Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, DeepSeek-V4Flash, Qwen3.8-27B, and K2 Horizon 375B A23B. If exposure helped, the later releases should lead at the idea level, where memorized content would matter most. They trail instead. Averaged over areas and methods, the two controls reach 3.10 on MATCH-IDEA against 1.68 for the 2026 releases, and Llama 4 Scout, with the earliest cutoff, scores highest of all six. The 2026 releases score slightly higher on MATCH-CITE, 5.06 against 4.14, but Claude Haiku 4.5 comes within 0.6 points of each of them, so this difference more plausibly reflects model capability than exposure. The two levels even move in opposite directions across models, as those with higher MATCH-CITE tend to have lower MATCH-IDEA. Access to the relevant literature is therefore not what limits recovery. Consistent findings in both settings. The findings of Sec. 4 hold in both groups. Matching stays far below the human level, at 22% on citations and 26% on ideas for the 2025 models and 28% and 14% for the 2026 releases. No population in either group reaches the human DIVERSITY-IDEA, and LANDSCAPE ranks last on MATCH-CITE in most settings of both. The only difference is the relatively high MATCH-IDEA of Llama 4 Scout, which runs against exposure rather than with it. Including the 2026 releases thus extends the evaluation to the latest models without changing its conclusions, and IdeaTaste, though built on time split, does not rest on memorization. Extending to later years. The construction of IdeaTaste repeats for any year by freezing the corpus at the end of 1, collecting the papers of as the reference, and applying the same metrics. Each new model can thus be evaluated against reference published after its training data end, which removes the concern altogether. Information access of LLM agents and human researchers. LLM agents can retrieve only literature published through 2025, whereas the 2026 papers are observed after the cutoff and their authors may have had access to work released during 2026. However, matching the information of an LLM agent to that of paper would require knowing what each author had read and restricting retrieval to it, which cannot be reconstructed after publication. IdeaTaste aligns what can be aligned. Every population searches the same corpus, which ends on the same date, and runs under the same budget, prompt, and judge, so this design leaves comparisons among LLM agents intact. The human level is read accordingly, as reference line for where research actually went rather than as competing arm under matched conditions.
